UNIT 19: POPULATION DYNAMICS

KEY THEME
- The world's population is dynamic (constantly changing). Studying size and distribution explains growth or decline and how people interact with environment and resources.
- Learning outcome: describe how physical landscape, natural resources, food, health, culture, gender equality and conflict affect population size and distribution in Ireland (Global North) and India (Global South).

GLOBAL NORTH AND GLOBAL SOUTH
- These terms refer to differences in wealth, development, education and opportunity, not strictly map position.
- Global North: developed, wealthier countries mostly in the Northern Hemisphere, e.g. Europe, North America, parts of Asia, Australia and New Zealand.
- Global South: developing and least developed countries, e.g. poorer countries in Africa, South America and Asia.
- The Brandt Line is a common way of showing the divide; there is no universal agreement on where some countries belong.

KEY TERMS
- Population: the total number of people living in an area, country or the world.
- Demography: the study of the size, growth, distribution and structure (age and gender) of a population and how these change.
- Birth rate: average number of live births per 1,000 people per year.
- Death rate: average number of deaths per 1,000 people per year.
- Total fertility rate (TFR): average number of children a woman has in her lifetime.
- Replacement rate: TFR needed for a population to stay the same size, usually 2.1.
- Migration: movement of people across borders; immigration adds, emigration reduces.
- Population density: average number of people per km2.
- Population distribution: how people are spread out across an area (the pattern of where they live).
- Even distribution: people spread out uniformly. Clustered distribution: people concentrated in certain areas. Sparse distribution: few people over large areas.
- Malnutrition: not getting the right balance of nutrients, causing tiredness, illness and poor growth.
- Famine: a severe, long-lasting shortage of food over a large area, often causing starvation and death.
- Food insecurity: no reliable access to safe, nutritious, affordable food.
- Life expectancy: the average number of years a person is expected to live.
- Territorial dispute: disagreement over ownership and control of land.
- Separatist movement: a group trying to break away and form its own state, often due to differences in ethnicity, culture, religion or history.
- Dowry: property or money brought by a bride to her husband on marriage.

POPULATION AND DEMOGRAPHY
- Four key factors: birth rate, death rate, TFR and migration. Together they decide growth or decline.
- Birth rates tend to be higher in developing countries where family planning is limited and culture or economics favour large families.
- Death rates tend to be lower in developed countries because of better healthcare and living conditions, so life expectancy is higher.
- If TFR falls below 2.1 the population ages and eventually decreases, as in many developed countries.
- Migration can fill labour shortages in receiver countries and ease overcrowding in donor countries. Ireland's growth today is strongly influenced by inward migration from Eastern Europe and beyond.
- Demographers study age structure, gender structure, migration and projections. In Ireland the CSO studies population.
- Demography helps governments plan schools, hospitals and homes; make health, education and welfare policies; tackle ageing populations or overcrowded cities; and promote sustainable development.
- Geofact: world population 8.3 billion (2026); India is the largest at 1,476,625,576.

FACTORS AFFECTING POPULATION SIZE AND DISTRIBUTION
- Physical landscape: higher densities where altitude is under 500 m; uplands are colder, have poor soils and are inaccessible. Higher densities in mid-latitudes 20 to 60 degrees with temperate climates. Low, scattered populations in hot deserts and tundras.
- Natural resources: water, fertile soil, minerals and fossil fuels provide jobs and support larger populations; areas lacking resources cannot support growth.
- Food: productive farming (good climate, relief, soil, drainage) supports high densities; steep, dry or thin-soiled land supports sparse populations. Reliable food lowers malnutrition and death rates; famine and food insecurity raise death rates and force migration.
- Health: clean water, sanitation and medical care raise life expectancy and lower death rates. The Global South lacks high-quality healthcare. People move to urban areas for better care.
- Culture: shared language and religion draw people together. Cultures valuing large families have high birth rates; others favour small families.
- Gender equality: equal access to education and work leads to lower birth rates, slower growth and higher life expectancy; families are smaller when women work outside the home. Early marriage raises birth rates.
- Conflict: people flee war zones (depopulation) to safe zones (overcrowding); death rates rise; birth rates fall due to uncertainty and separated families. Long conflicts change age and gender structures.

CASE STUDY: IRELAND (GLOBAL NORTH)
- Uneven distribution: east and south high density; west and northwest low density. Island of Ireland population 6.8 million.
- Physical landscape: low density in uplands with steep slopes, harsh weather and poor soil, e.g. as low as 25 per km2 in MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Kerry. Midlands and Shannon Basin have poorly drained soils. The fertile Golden Vale in Tipperary also has low density because highly productive farming dominates.
- High density around urban areas, coastal lowlands and well-drained river valleys (e.g. Liffey Valley), and at river mouths where towns and ports grew.
- 2022 census: Greater Dublin Area about 1.3 million; Dublin City about 593,000 at about 5,000 per km2, by far the densest city.
- Natural resources: fertile soils in Kildare and Meath support large rural populations. Meath potatoes supply Tayto Snacks (400-500 jobs nationwide). Dublin, Cork and Limerick grew as centres of trade and industry. The Kinsale Head Gas Field (about 50 km off the south coast in the Celtic Sea) powered Cork's industries; Cork is the second-largest city. The west and northwest lack resources and industrial jobs, so densities are low.
- Food: the Great Famine (1845-1852) caused massive decline: 8.2 million (1841) to 6.5 million (1851) to 3.2 million by the early 1900s, through deaths and emigration. Rural populations fell while towns grew. Map 1841-1851 shows falls of over 30% in some areas, with a few areas rising.
- From the 1900s, better food availability, living standards and less emigration let population grow. Modern farming (milking machines, combine harvesters, fertilisers, pesticides), refrigerated transport and supermarkets made food reliable, supporting growth in towns and cities.
- Health: Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway have hospitals and specialist care (e.g. the new National Children's Hospital), raising life expectancy and attracting families and workers. Mayo and Donegal have fewer facilities despite ageing populations; this encourages young people to leave. Only 10% of Irish GPs work in rural areas.
- Culture (religion): Catholicism encouraged large families and high birth rates; church and state were closely aligned. 1973 amendment removed the Church's special status. Contraception not easily available until 1985; abortion legalised in 2018. Birth rates fell from the 1990s. Catholicism is stronger among older rural people; migration has brought Islam, Hinduism and Orthodox Christianity mainly to cities.
- Culture (language): after the 1950s Irish was mainly spoken in Gaeltacht areas of Galway, Kerry and Donegal. Lack of jobs led young people to leave, so Connemara and Ballyferriter declined. Ireland grew from about 2.8 million (1950s) to about 5.3 million (2025), mostly in urban areas.
- Gender equality: 1920s-1960s married women expected to stay home; the Marriage Bar (until 1973) stopped female teachers and civil servants working after marriage. 1961: 60% of adult women in 'home duties', only 9% of married women employed; TFR 3.78; first child at 24. Change from the 1970s: women's liberation, joining the EU, equal pay and education laws. 2024 CSO: first-time mothers average 31.7 years; TFR 1.5 (below 2.1). Over 70% of women now in paid work or seeking it. Families fell from over four children (1960s) to 1.5 (2024). Examples of successful women: Rhasidat Adeleke and Norah Patten.
- Conflict: War of Independence (1919-1921) and Civil War (1922-1923) caused deaths, displacement and emigration, deepening rural decline and urban growth. Today, the war in Ukraine (from 2022): under the EU Temporary Protection scheme Ireland gave Ukrainians housing, education and work; 70,000 arrived by April 2023, especially in Dublin, Cork, Kerry and Louth.

CASE STUDY: INDIA (GLOBAL SOUTH)
- Over 1.4 billion people, the most populated country. Very uneven: Himalayan uplands very low density; Ganges Plain very high.
- Physical landscape: the Ganges Plain has flat land and fertile alluvial soil for intensive farming. Uttar Pradesh, on the plain, is the most populous state (over 240 million) with 828 people per km2, more than double the national average. The Himalayas average 33 per km2 (harsh terrain, cold, inaccessible, hard to farm or build roads). The Thar Desert in Rajasthan has a dry climate and sandy soil; settlements are scattered and many people are nomadic.
- Natural resources: Uttar Pradesh's alluvial soil and Ganges water support rice and wheat; labour-intensive farming gives stable jobs. Jute on the Ganges Delta in West Bengal supports a labour-intensive textile industry, attracting migrants (very high density). Odisha's coal and iron ore support mining and iron and steel industry. Khetri, Rajasthan has one of India's largest copper mines; population grew about 50% in 20 years (17,377 in 2001; 18,209 in 2011; 25,000 in 2023; 26,400 in 2025).
- Food: the Green Revolution (1960s) used irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides and high-yielding crops. Punjab wheat rose from about 1 million tonnes (1950) to over 10 million tonnes (1985). Fewer hunger deaths, more children survived, longer life expectancy, more services. Bihar benefited less, suffering food shortages and rural-urban migration. The Public Distribution System (PDS) buys rice and wheat and sells it cheaply through Fair Price Shops to poor families; food security still varies (Punjab more secure than Bihar).
- Health: by 2018, 98.7% had access to clean water and sanitation, reducing cholera, typhoid and gastroenteritis. Kerala has one of the lowest death rates (6 per 1,000 live births) and highest life expectancy (over 74) thanks to state vaccination and nutrition programmes; it attracts migrants. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar have underfunded, overcrowded hospitals; life expectancy in Uttar Pradesh is 10 years less than Kerala and infant mortality five times higher. People migrate to Mumbai and Delhi for healthcare.
- Culture: in northern states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) traditional Hindu values favour large families and early marriage, giving rapid growth. 'Son preference' (sons carry the family name and care for parents; daughters leave and need a dowry) affects family size and sex ratio. Kerala and Tamil Nadu are more progressive: lower birth rates, smaller families, later marriage, balanced sex ratio. Hindi speakers concentrate in the north, Tamil speakers in the south; Mumbai and Delhi are mixed.
- Gender equality: Bihar female literacy as low as 60% and early marriage give a fertility rate of 3.0, double Kerala or Tamil Nadu. 23% of Indian girls are married by 18. Kerala: female literacy 97%, fertility 1.7, close to Irish levels; more girls finish school and more women work. Mumbai and Bangalore grow fast and are more gender-equal.
- Conflict: Partition in 1947 created Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority West and East Pakistan (Bangladesh from 1971); about 1 million deaths and over 14 million displaced. Kashmir: hundreds of thousands fled the Kashmir Valley in the 1990s to Delhi and Jammu. Northeast: ethnic violence and separatist movements; in Manipur in 2024, 70 killed and 60,000 left, many to refugee camps or Delhi, causing urban overcrowding and slums while conflict areas shrink.

SUMMARY POINTS
- Population change depends on births, deaths and migration.
- Density examples: Dublin high; MacGillycuddy's Reeks low. Himalayas sparse; Ganges Plain dense.
- India has a youthful population structure; Ireland an ageing one.

rows.prompt: What do the terms Global North and Global South mainly describe?
options: Which hemisphere a country is in
rows.explanation: They refer to differences in wealth, development, education and opportunities, not strictly map position.

rows.prompt: What is the Brandt Line?
options: The border between India and Pakistan
A line of equal population density
A line showing a common Global North and South divide
rows.explanation: The Brandt Line is a common depiction of the divide between the Global North and South.

rows.prompt: What is the birth rate?
options: Average children per woman in her lifetime
Live births per 1,000 people per year
Number of babies born in a hospital
rows.explanation: Birth rate is the average number of live births per 1,000 people per year.

rows.prompt: What is the replacement level of total fertility rate?
rows.explanation: A TFR of 2.1 keeps a population stable from one generation to the next.

rows.prompt: What happens if a country's TFR stays below 2.1 with no migration?
rows.explanation: Below 2.1 the population begins to age and eventually decreases.

rows.prompt: Which body studies population growth in Ireland?
rows.explanation: The Central Statistics Office (CSO) is responsible for studying population in Ireland.

rows.prompt: What is population density?
options: The total number of people in a country
The pattern of where people live
Average number of people per km2
The age and gender make-up of people
rows.explanation: Population density is the average number of people per km2.

rows.prompt: Below what altitude are larger population densities usually found?
rows.explanation: Larger population densities are found where altitude is less than 500 m.

rows.prompt: Between which latitudes are population densities higher?
rows.explanation: The mid-latitudes between 20 and 60 degrees have temperate climates and productive farming.

rows.prompt: How does gender equality usually affect population?
options: Higher birth rates and faster growth
Higher death rates and lower life expectancy
Lower birth rates and slower growth
More early marriage and larger families
rows.explanation: Equal education and work for women lowers birth rates, slows growth and raises life expectancy.

rows.prompt: Why does the Golden Vale have low population density despite fertile soil?
options: Highly productive farming dominates the land
It is too high and cold for settlement
It has no roads or railways
rows.explanation: Settlement is discouraged because highly productive farming dominates.

rows.prompt: What is the population density in MacGillycuddy's Reeks?
rows.explanation: Density is as low as 25 people per km2 in MacGillycuddy's Reeks.

rows.prompt: Which energy resource helped Cork's industries grow?
rows.explanation: The Kinsale Head Gas Field in the Celtic Sea powered local industries and attracted workers.

rows.prompt: What is the approximate population density of Dublin City?
rows.explanation: Dublin City has about 593,000 people at roughly 5,000 per km2.

rows.prompt: What was Ireland's population in 1841, before the Great Famine?
rows.explanation: It fell from 8.2 million in 1841 to 6.5 million in 1851 and 3.2 million by the early 1900s.

rows.prompt: What share of Irish GPs work in rural areas?
rows.explanation: The Geofact states only 10% of Irish GPs work in rural areas.

rows.prompt: What was the Marriage Bar?
options: A law stopping some women working after marriage
A rule setting the minimum age for marriage
A tax on married couples with children
A ban on marriage between religions
rows.explanation: Until 1973 it prevented female teachers and civil servants from working after marriage.

rows.prompt: What was Ireland's fertility rate in 2024?
rows.explanation: CSO figures for 2024 show 1.5 children per woman, well below replacement.

rows.prompt: What was the average age of first-time mothers in Ireland in 2024?
rows.explanation: The 2024 CSO average was 31.7 years, up from 24 in 1961.

rows.prompt: Why have Gaeltacht populations, such as in Connemara, declined?
options: The land was flooded by new reservoirs
Government policy moved people to Dublin
Families moved for better Irish schools
Young people left because jobs were hard to find
rows.explanation: Jobs became harder to find so young people left for cities or abroad.

rows.prompt: How many Ukrainians had arrived in Ireland by April 2023?
rows.explanation: By April 2023, 70,000 Ukrainians had arrived seeking refuge.

rows.prompt: Which Indian region has very high population density?
rows.explanation: The low-lying Ganges Plain with fertile alluvial soil has very high density.

rows.prompt: What is the population density of Uttar Pradesh?
rows.explanation: Uttar Pradesh has 828 people per km2, more than double the national average.

rows.prompt: Why do many people in the Thar Desert live a nomadic lifestyle?
options: To search for water and food
To follow tourists around the region
To avoid flooding from the Ganges
rows.explanation: The dry climate and sandy soil mean people move from place to place for water and food.

rows.prompt: What caused Khetri, Rajasthan to grow by about 50% in 20 years?
rows.explanation: Khetri has one of India's largest copper mines and grew through mining and industry.

rows.prompt: What was the Green Revolution?
options: A campaign to plant forests across India
A move from farming to factory work
Use of irrigation, fertilisers and high-yielding crops
A ban on pesticides in Indian farming
rows.explanation: It used irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides with high-yielding crops to boost wheat and rice yields.

rows.prompt: How did Punjab's wheat production change from 1950 to 1985?
options: Rose from 1 to over 10 million tonnes
rows.explanation: Punjab's wheat rose from about 1 million tonnes in 1950 to over 10 million tonnes by 1985.

rows.prompt: Why does Kerala have high life expectancy?
options: Its location in the cool Himalayas
Large numbers of mines providing jobs
A state-run vaccination and nutrition programme
rows.explanation: Kerala's state vaccination and nutrition programme lowered infant mortality; life expectancy is over 74.

rows.prompt: What is 'son preference'?
options: A law giving sons more land than daughters
A school system for boys only
A tax break for families with sons
A belief that sons will carry the family name and care for parents
rows.explanation: It is a traditional belief that a son carries on the name and looks after parents in old age.

rows.prompt: What is Bihar's fertility rate compared with Kerala's?
rows.explanation: Low female literacy and early marriage give Bihar 3.0; Kerala's 97% female literacy gives 1.7.

rows.prompt: How many people were displaced by the Partition of India in 1947?
rows.explanation: Partition caused an estimated 1 million deaths and displaced over 14 million people.

rows.prompt: Name the four key factors that decide whether a population grows or declines.
rows.model_answer: The four key factors are birth rate, death rate, total fertility rate and migration. High birth rates and immigration increase population, while high death rates and emigration reduce it. A TFR below 2.1 leads to an ageing, declining population.

rows.prompt: Explain why demography is useful to governments.
rows.model_answer: Demography helps governments plan for future needs like schools, hospitals and homes. It informs policies on healthcare, education and social welfare. It helps tackle challenges such as ageing populations or overcrowded cities and supports sustainable development.

rows.prompt: Explain how the physical landscape affects population distribution in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Uplands like MacGillycuddy's Reeks have steep slopes, harsh weather and poor soil, so density is as low as 25 per km2. The midlands and Shannon Basin have poorly drained soils that discourage settlement. Flat, fertile coastal lowlands and river valleys like the Liffey Valley support high densities, especially at river mouths where ports grew.

rows.prompt: Describe the impact of the Great Famine on Ireland's population.
rows.model_answer: The Great Famine (1845-1852) caused massive decline through high death rates and emigration. Population fell from 8.2 million in 1841 to 6.5 million in 1851 and 3.2 million by the early 1900s. Rural populations fell while towns and cities grew, changing distribution.

rows.prompt: Explain how improved gender equality has changed Ireland's population.
rows.model_answer: In 1961 only 9% of married women worked outside the home and the fertility rate was 3.78. From the 1970s women gained equal pay, education and job rights, and over 70% now work or seek work. Women delay or limit children, so the fertility rate fell to 1.5 in 2024 and the average first-time mother is 31.7.

rows.prompt: Compare population density on the Ganges Plain and in the Himalayas.
rows.model_answer: The Ganges Plain has flat land and fertile alluvial soil for intensive farming; Uttar Pradesh has 828 people per km2. The Himalayas have steep terrain, a cold climate and poor access, making farming and building hard, so the average is only 33 per km2.

rows.prompt: Explain how the Green Revolution affected India's population.
rows.model_answer: The Green Revolution of the 1960s used irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides and high-yielding crops. Wheat in Punjab rose from about 1 million to over 10 million tonnes. Fewer people died of hunger, more children survived and life expectancy rose, so population grew. Bihar benefited less and suffered shortages and out-migration.

rows.prompt: Contrast Kerala and Bihar in terms of gender equality and fertility.
rows.model_answer: Bihar has female literacy as low as 60% and common early marriage, giving a fertility rate of 3.0. Kerala has 97% female literacy, more girls finishing school and more women working, so its fertility rate is just 1.7. Kerala has slower growth and healthier children.

rows.prompt: Describe how conflict has affected population distribution in India.
rows.model_answer: Partition in 1947 caused about 1 million deaths and displaced over 14 million people. Hundreds of thousands fled the Kashmir Valley in the 1990s to Delhi and Jammu. In Manipur in 2024, 70 were killed and 60,000 left. Conflict areas shrink while safer cities become overcrowded with slums.

rows.prompt: Examine the impact of two of the following factors on population size and distribution in Ireland: natural resources, food, health. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Natural resources: Fertile soils in Kildare and Meath support large rural populations, and Meath potatoes supply Tayto Snacks, which employs 400-500 people. Dublin, Cork and Limerick grew as centres of trade and industry around ports and resources. The Kinsale Head Gas Field, about 50 km off the south coast, powered Cork's industries and attracted workers, making Cork the second-largest city. The west and northwest lack resources and industrial jobs, so they are sparsely populated. Health: Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway have hospitals and specialist care, such as the new National Children's Hospital, which raises life expectancy and attracts families and healthcare workers. Mayo and Donegal have fewer hospitals despite ageing populations, as it is hard to justify facilities where people are scattered. Only 10% of GPs work in rural areas. This makes rural areas unattractive and young people leave, so rural populations decline and age while cities grow.
rows.marking_scheme: Factor 1 named 2m + 6 SRPs x 2m. Factor 2 named 2m + 6 SRPs x 2m. Credit Irish examples and statistics. Max 30 marks (allow 1 overall SRP for linking to distribution).

rows.prompt: Examine how the physical landscape and natural resources affect population distribution in a Global South country you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: India has over 1.4 billion people with a very uneven distribution. The Ganges Plain has flat land and fertile alluvial soil, supporting intensive farming. Uttar Pradesh, on the plain, is the most populous state with over 240 million people and 828 per km2, more than double the national average. The Himalayas have steep, rugged terrain, a cold climate and poor access; building roads and houses is very hard and farming is difficult, so density averages only 33 per km2. The Thar Desert in Rajasthan has a dry climate and sandy soil, so settlements are scattered and many people are nomadic. Natural resources also attract people. Uttar Pradesh's alluvial soil and water from the Ganges grow rice and wheat, and labour-intensive farming gives stable jobs. Jute on the Ganges Delta in West Bengal supports a labour-intensive textile industry that attracts migrants. Odisha's coal and iron ore support mining and iron and steel. Khetri in Rajasthan has one of India's largest copper mines and its population grew about 50% in 20 years, from 17,377 in 2001 to 26,400 in 2025.
rows.marking_scheme: Named country 2m. Physical landscape: 7 SRPs x 2m. Natural resources: 7 SRPs x 2m. Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Compare the influence of gender equality on population in Ireland and India. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: In Ireland, from the 1920s to 1960s married women were expected to stay home and the Marriage Bar, in place until 1973, stopped female teachers and civil servants working after marriage. In 1961, 60% of adult women were in home duties, only 9% of married women worked, the fertility rate was 3.78 and women had their first child at 24. From the 1970s the women's liberation movement, joining the EU and equal pay and education laws gave women more opportunities. Now over 70% work or seek work, the average first-time mother is 31.7 and the fertility rate is 1.5, below replacement. In India there is huge regional variation. In Bihar, female literacy is as low as 60% and early marriage is common, giving a fertility rate of 3.0; 23% of Indian girls marry by 18. Son preference also increases family size. In Kerala, female literacy is 97% and the fertility rate is 1.7, close to Irish levels, with more girls finishing school and working. In both countries, more equality for women means smaller families and slower growth, but much of India is at an earlier stage than Ireland.
rows.marking_scheme: Ireland: 7 SRPs x 2m. India: 7 SRPs x 2m. Comparison point 2m. Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Describe the impact of conflict on population size and distribution, with reference to Ireland and/or India. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Conflict raises death rates, lowers birth rates and forces people to move. In Ireland, the War of Independence (1919-1921) and Civil War (1922-1923) caused deaths, displacement and emigration, deepening rural decline and urban growth. Today the war in Ukraine has affected Ireland: under the EU Temporary Protection scheme, 70,000 Ukrainians had arrived by April 2023, mainly in Dublin, Cork, Kerry and Louth. In India, Partition in 1947 caused about 1 million deaths and displaced over 14 million people. Hundreds of thousands fled the Kashmir Valley in the 1990s to Delhi and Jammu. In Manipur in 2024, 70 were killed and 60,000 left, many to camps or Delhi, causing overcrowding and slums while conflict areas lost people.
rows.marking_scheme: 10 SRPs x 2m. Named conflicts and statistics count as SRPs. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain how health affects population size and distribution in India. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Improved water and sanitation have driven rapid growth: by 2018, 98.7% of Indians had access to clean water and sanitation, reducing cholera, typhoid and gastroenteritis, lowering death rates and raising life expectancy. Kerala has one of the lowest death rates (6 per 1,000 live births) and life expectancy over 74 because of its state-run vaccination and nutrition programme. It has a stable population and attracts migrants from other states. In Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, hospitals are underfunded, overcrowded and understaffed; life expectancy in Uttar Pradesh is 10 years less than Kerala and infant mortality is five times higher. Poor services push people to cities like Mumbai and Delhi, which grow quickly, while rural regions have slower growth and older populations.
rows.marking_scheme: 10 SRPs x 2m. Named states and statistics count as SRPs. Max 20 marks.
